content.summary:
## Overview

EBS (Elastic Block Store) is a network-attached block drive for EC2 that persists data independently of instance lifetime, but is locked to a single Availability Zone and mounted to one instance at a time. The exam tests the consequences of those constraints: how you bill provisioned size and IOPS, why a snapshot is the only path to move or copy a volume across AZs or Regions, and what happens to volumes when an instance terminates. On top of snapshots sit three features — Archive (cheap, slow restore), Recycle Bin (recover deleted snapshots for 1 day to 1 year) and Fast Snapshot Restore (remove first-use latency for a price) — that are classic cost-vs-latency and recovery scenarios.

## Core Concepts

- **EBS Volume:** A network drive (not a physical drive) that you attach to an EC2 instance while it runs, letting the instance persist data even after termination; often described as a "network USB stick".
- **Network drive latency:** Because EBS communicates with the instance over the network, there may be a bit of latency compared with instance storage.
- **Attach/detach behavior:** An EBS volume can be detached from one EC2 instance and attached to another quickly; at the CCP level it can only be mounted to one instance at a time.
- **AZ-bound volume:** An EBS volume is locked to a specific Availability Zone — a volume in us-east-1a cannot be attached to an instance in us-east-1b; moving across AZs requires a snapshot.
- **Provisioned capacity:** A volume has provisioned capacity (size in GB and IOPS) that you choose up front; capacity can be increased over time.
- **Provisioned-capacity billing:** You are billed for all the provisioned capacity, regardless of how much of it the instance actually uses.
- **EBS Snapshot:** A point-in-time backup of an EBS volume; detaching the volume first is not necessary but is recommended.
- **Snapshot copy across AZ or Region:** Snapshots can be copied across Availability Zones or Regions, and restoring a snapshot in another AZ creates a volume there — the standard way to move a volume.
- **Delete on Termination attribute:** An EBS attribute controlling what happens to the volume when the attached EC2 instance terminates; controllable via AWS console or AWS CLI.
- **Root volume default deletion:** By default the root EBS volume is deleted on instance termination (attribute enabled); by default any other attached EBS volume is not deleted (attribute disabled).
- **EBS Snapshot Archive:** Moves a snapshot to an "archive tier" that is 75% cheaper, with restore taking within 24 to 72 hours.
- **Recycle Bin for EBS Snapshots:** Rules that retain deleted snapshots so you can recover them after an accidental deletion; retention is specified from 1 day to 1 year.
- **Fast Snapshot Restore (FSR):** Forces full initialization of a snapshot so a restored volume has no latency on first use; costs extra ($$$).

## Key Comparisons

- **EBS volume vs instance store:** EBS is a network drive that persists independently of the instance; an instance store is tied to the physical host and does not survive the way a detachable network drive does.
- **Same-AZ attach vs cross-AZ move:** Within one AZ a volume can be detached and re-attached quickly; across AZs you must snapshot and restore.
- **Root volume vs non-root volume on termination:** Root volume is deleted by default; additional data volumes are kept by default.
- **EBS Snapshot vs EBS Snapshot Archive:** Standard snapshots restore quickly; archive copies are 75% cheaper but take 24-72 hours to restore.
- **EBS Snapshot Archive vs Recycle Bin:** Archive is a cheap long-term storage tier for snapshots you keep; Recycle Bin retains snapshots you deleted so they can be recovered (1 day-1 year).
- **Recycle Bin vs Fast Snapshot Restore:** Recycle Bin answers "I deleted it by accident"; FSR answers "restore is too slow on first use" and is paid for with extra cost.
- **Snapshot taken without detach vs after detach:** Both are possible — detaching is optional but recommended for a clean point-in-time backup.
- **Provisioned vs used capacity:** Billing follows provisioned GB and IOPS, so over-provisioning costs money even when idle.

## Common Misunderstandings

- An EBS volume can be attached to instances in any AZ in the Region — it cannot; it is locked to its AZ.
- You only pay for the storage you fill up — you pay for all provisioned capacity, including provisioned IOPS.
- All attached volumes are deleted when the instance terminates — only the root volume is deleted by default.
- You must detach a volume before you can snapshot it — you need not, though it is recommended.
- Snapshots are AZ-bound like volumes — snapshots can be copied across AZs and Regions.
- Deleting a snapshot is always final — a Recycle Bin rule can retain deleted snapshots from 1 day to 1 year.
- Archive tier is just cheaper snapshots with the same restore time — restore from archive takes 24 to 72 hours.
- FSR makes the snapshot smaller or cheaper — FSR forces full initialization to remove first-use latency and costs extra.

## Mental Models

- Think of EBS as a "network USB stick": you plug it into an instance, unplug and move it — but only within the same AZ.
- Think of the AZ as the building the drive is physically locked inside; to get it into another building you ship a copy (the snapshot).
- Think of billing as renting a parking space by size and speed, not by how often you park.
- Think of Delete on Termination as a checkbox on each volume: on for the root by default, off for the others.
- Think of Snapshot Archive as the cold warehouse, Recycle Bin as the trash can with an undo window, and FSR as paying to pre-warm the engine.

## Exceptions & Edge Cases

- A volume can be unattached entirely (shown as unattached alongside instances in different AZs) — an unattached volume still incurs provisioned-capacity billing.
- Delete on Termination is per-volume, so you can run a non-root volume with it enabled or a root volume with it disabled.
- Use case for disabling it on the root volume: preserve the root volume when the instance is terminated.
- Archive restore time is a range (24 to 72 hours), not a fixed value, and cannot be shortened by FSR.
- Recycle Bin must be set up with rules in advance — retention of 1 day to 1 year applies only to snapshots covered by a rule.
- Snapshotting a live volume is allowed without detaching, so an exam option that makes detaching mandatory is wrong.
- FSR costs extra ($$$), so it is a latency-requirement choice, not a cost-optimization choice.

## When to Use Which

- Data must survive the termination of the EC2 instance it is attached to → **EBS volume instead of ephemeral instance storage**
- A volume must be used by an instance in a different Availability Zone → **Snapshot the volume and restore it as a new volume in the target AZ**
- Copy a workload's volume to another Region → **Copy the snapshot across the Region, then restore**
- Keep the root volume after the instance is terminated → **Disable the Delete on Termination attribute on the root volume**
- Keep a rarely accessed backup at minimum cost and slow restore is acceptable → **Move the snapshot to EBS Snapshot Archive (75% cheaper, restore in 24-72 hours)**
- Protect against accidental deletion of snapshots for a defined period → **Recycle Bin for EBS Snapshots with a retention of 1 day to 1 year**
- Restored volumes must have no latency on first use → **Enable Fast Snapshot Restore, accepting the extra cost**

## Patterns to Recognize

- "Volume in us-east-1a must be used by an instance in us-east-1b" → **EBS is AZ-bound; snapshot + restore**
- "Move data to another Region" → **Snapshot copy across Regions, then restore**
- "Billed for capacity not used" → **Provisioned GB and IOPS billing**
- "Instance was terminated and the data volume disappeared" → **Delete on Termination on the root volume (default enabled)**
- "Cheapest backup of snapshots that are rarely restored" → **EBS Snapshot Archive**
- "Snapshot was deleted by mistake — recover it" → **Recycle Bin for EBS Snapshots (retention 1 day-1 year)**
- "High latency on first read after restoring from snapshot" → **Fast Snapshot Restore (full initialization, extra cost)**
- "Within 24 to 72 hours" → **Archive tier restore time**
- "Backup needs a clean point-in-time, no downtime required" → **Snapshot without detaching (detach recommended, not required)**

## Exam Traps

- “Pick a volume in another AZ and attach it directly.” — A volume cannot cross AZs; snapshot it and restore in the target AZ.
- “Choose the smallest volume to save money.” — Billing is on provisioned size and IOPS, so size/IOPS should match the requirement, not be minimized.
- “Assume all volumes are deleted at termination.” — Only the root volume is deleted by default; other volumes persist (attribute disabled).
- “Say snapshotting requires the volume to be detached first.” — Detaching is not necessary, only recommended.
- “Use Archive for a workload needing fast restore.” — Archive restore takes 24 to 72 hours; use a standard snapshot (or FSR) when speed matters.
- “Use Fast Snapshot Restore to reduce snapshot storage cost.” — FSR removes first-use latency and costs extra; use Archive for cost reduction.
- “Expect Recycle Bin to retain snapshots indefinitely.” — Retention is set by rule and ranges from 1 day to 1 year.
- “Assume an unattached volume is free.” — Provisioned capacity is billed whether or not the volume is attached.

## Beyond the Source (tutor knowledge)

- (Tutor knowledge) The source says one instance at a time "at the CCP level"; on the SAA exam, multi-attach is a fact for specific EBS volume types (io1/io2) in the same AZ, and is still not a way to cross AZs.
- (Tutor knowledge) EBS volume types (gp2/gp3, io1/io2, st1, sc1) are examinable under SAA "block storage options (HDD vs SSD)" and "selecting the appropriate storage tier"; the AZ lock and snapshot mechanics on this page apply to all of them.

You are billed for the full provisioned capacity (GBs and IOPS), not for the portion used.
Volume capacity can be increased over time; provisioned size/IOPS is a chosen quantity, not a ceiling on usage.
By default, the root EBS volume IS deleted when the instance terminates (Delete on Termination enabled).
By default, non-root attached EBS volumes are NOT deleted when the instance terminates (attribute disabled).
Delete on Termination can be changed via the AWS console or AWS CLI — e.g. to preserve the root volume.
Detaching a volume before snapshotting is not required, but is recommended.
EBS Snapshot Archive is 75% cheaper and restores within 24 to 72 hours.
Recycle Bin retention for deleted snapshots is from 1 day to 1 year.
Fast Snapshot Restore removes first-use latency by full initialization of the snapshot, and costs extra.

quiz.question: A company runs a database on an EC2 instance in us-east-1a. A new analytics instance is launched in us-east-1b and must use the same data. What is the correct approach?
options: Detach the volume and attach it to the instance in us-east-1b
Take a snapshot of the volume and restore it as a new volume in us-east-1b
Create a new empty volume in us-east-1b and copy files over the network
Enable Delete on Termination on the volume so it can be recreated in us-east-1b
quiz.explanation: An EBS volume is locked to its Availability Zone, so the only supported way to move data across AZs is to snapshot it and restore the snapshot as a new volume in the target AZ. Detaching and re-attaching keeps the volume in us-east-1a and it cannot attach in us-east-1b; a new empty volume plus network copy is not the standard mechanism and adds avoidable work; Delete on Termination controls deletion at instance termination and has nothing to do with AZ placement.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes an EBS volume?
options: A physical disk that is part of the host running the instance
A network drive attached to an instance that persists data after termination
An object store bucket mountable by many instances simultaneously
A local buffer that is erased whenever the instance stops
quiz.explanation: EBS is a network drive ('network USB stick') attached to an instance over the network, and it persists data even after the instance terminates. It is not a physical drive on the host; S3 is the object store, and EBS is block storage bound to one instance at a time at the foundational level; it is not an ephemeral local buffer.

quiz.question: A team provisioned a 1 TB EBS volume with high provisioned IOPS but the application only fills 200 GB and rarely drives IOPS. How is billing calculated?
options: For the 200 GB actually stored and the IOPS actually consumed
For the full provisioned size and provisioned IOPS
For provisioned size only, with IOPS included at no charge
For used capacity only, since an unattached volume is free
quiz.explanation: EBS bills all provisioned capacity — both provisioned GB and provisioned IOPS — regardless of actual use, so over-provisioning costs money even when idle. Billing is not based on stored data or consumed IOPS; IOPS are not free with a volume; and an unattached or lightly used volume is still billed for its provisioned capacity.

quiz.question: A web server instance is terminated and the team notices that its root volume disappeared while a separately attached data volume remained. Which behaviour explains this?
options: The root volume had Delete on Termination enabled by default; the data volume had it disabled by default
All attached volumes are deleted on termination unless they are re-attached within an hour
The data volume survived only because it was larger than the root volume
Volumes survive termination only if an EBS snapshot was taken in the last 24 hours
quiz.explanation: Delete on Termination is enabled by default on the root volume (so it is deleted) and disabled by default on other attached volumes (so they persist); the attribute can be changed via the console or AWS CLI. There is no re-attach grace period; volume size does not determine deletion; and snapshots do not change the termination behaviour of a volume.

quiz.question: An architect must keep the root volume of an EC2 instance after the instance is terminated. What is the recommended action?
options: Copy the root volume to a snapshot before each boot
Disable the Delete on Termination attribute on the root volume
Attach the root volume to a second instance as a data volume
Enable Fast Snapshot Restore on the root volume's snapshot
quiz.explanation: Delete on Termination is a per-volume attribute, and disabling it on the root volume is the documented use case for preserving the root volume when the instance terminates. Snapshotting before each boot is unnecessary overhead and not a guarantee of preservation; a root volume cannot simply be attached as a data volume of another instance; FSR reduces first-use restore latency and does not affect termination.

quiz.question: A company needs a long-term backup of a rarely restored EBS volume and wants the lowest storage cost, accepting that recovery may take a day or more. Which option fits?
options: Keep a standard EBS snapshot in the Region
Move the snapshot to EBS Snapshot Archive
Enable Fast Snapshot Restore on the snapshot
Configure a Recycle Bin rule for deleted snapshots
quiz.explanation: EBS Snapshot Archive moves the snapshot to an archive tier that is 75% cheaper, at the cost of a restore time of within 24 to 72 hours — acceptable when speed is not required. A standard snapshot costs more to keep; FSR removes first-use latency and costs extra, the opposite of cost saving; Recycle Bin retains deleted snapshots and does not reduce storage cost of a snapshot you intend to keep.

quiz.question: An administrator accidentally deleted a production EBS snapshot yesterday. What should have been configured in advance to recover it?
options: A Recycle Bin rule retaining deleted snapshots for a chosen period between 1 day and 1 year
EBS Snapshot Archive on the snapshot with a 24 to 72 hour restore window
Fast Snapshot Restore on the volume that was restored from the snapshot
Delete on Termination disabled on the snapshot's source volume
quiz.explanation: Recycle Bin for EBS Snapshots uses rules that retain deleted snapshots so they can be recovered, with a retention period from 1 day to 1 year, and the rules must be set up before the deletion. Archive is a cheaper storage tier, not an undelete mechanism; FSR addresses first-use latency of restored volumes; Delete on Termination governs volumes at instance termination, not snapshots.

quiz.question: After restoring a volume from a snapshot, an application shows high latency on its first reads until the data is fully accessed. Which feature addresses this requirement?
options: EBS Snapshot Archive, which pre-loads the snapshot to the target AZ
Fast Snapshot Restore, which forces full initialization at extra cost
A Recycle Bin rule that keeps the snapshot for 1 year
Delete on Termination enabled on the restored volume
quiz.explanation: Fast Snapshot Restore forces full initialization of the snapshot so the restored volume has no latency on first use, and it costs extra ($$$). Archive is a cheaper tier with a 24 to 72 hour restore and does not pre-load data; Recycle Bin only retains deleted snapshots; Delete on Termination has no effect on read latency.

quiz.question: Which comparison between EBS Snapshot Archive and Fast Snapshot Restore is correct?
options: Archive reduces storage cost but slows restore; FSR removes first-use latency but increases cost
Archive removes first-use latency; FSR reduces storage cost by 75%
Both reduce cost, and both restore within 24 to 72 hours
Both require the volume to be detached before use
quiz.explanation: Archive trades restore speed for cost (75% cheaper, restore within 24 to 72 hours), while FSR trades money for speed (full initialization, no first-use latency, extra cost) — they solve opposite problems. The roles are not reversed; neither option describes two cost reducers or a common 24 to 72 hour window; and detaching is not required for snapshots in either case, only recommended.

keyComparisons.difference: Both are possible — detaching is optional but recommended for a clean point-in-time backup.
Billing follows provisioned GB and IOPS, so over-provisioning costs money even when idle.

commonMisunderstandings: An EBS volume can be attached to instances in any AZ in the Region — it cannot; it is locked to its AZ.
You only pay for the storage you fill up — you pay for all provisioned capacity, including provisioned IOPS.
All attached volumes are deleted when the instance terminates — only the root volume is deleted by default.
You must detach a volume before you can snapshot it — you need not, though it is recommended.
Snapshots are AZ-bound like volumes — snapshots can be copied across AZs and Regions.
Deleting a snapshot is always final — a Recycle Bin rule can retain deleted snapshots from 1 day to 1 year.
Archive tier is just cheaper snapshots with the same restore time — restore from archive takes 24 to 72 hours.
FSR makes the snapshot smaller or cheaper — FSR forces full initialization to remove first-use latency and costs extra.
mentalModels: Think of EBS as a "network USB stick": you plug it into an instance, unplug and move it — but only within the same AZ.
Think of the AZ as the building the drive is physically locked inside; to get it into another building you ship a copy (the snapshot).
Think of billing as renting a parking space by size and speed, not by how often you park.
Think of Delete on Termination as a checkbox on each volume: on for the root by default, off for the others.
Think of Snapshot Archive as the cold warehouse, Recycle Bin as the trash can with an undo window, and FSR as paying to pre-warm the engine.
edgeCases: A volume can be unattached entirely (shown as unattached alongside instances in different AZs) — an unattached volume still incurs provisioned-capacity billing.
Delete on Termination is per-volume, so you can run a non-root volume with it enabled or a root volume with it disabled.
Use case for disabling it on the root volume: preserve the root volume when the instance is terminated.
Archive restore time is a range (24 to 72 hours), not a fixed value, and cannot be shortened by FSR.
Recycle Bin must be set up with rules in advance — retention of 1 day to 1 year applies only to snapshots covered by a rule.
Snapshotting a live volume is allowed without detaching, so an exam option that makes detaching mandatory is wrong.
FSR costs extra ($$$), so it is a latency-requirement choice, not a cost-optimization choice.

examTraps.trap: Pick a volume in another AZ and attach it directly.
examTraps.correction: A volume cannot cross AZs; snapshot it and restore in the target AZ.

examTraps.trap: Choose the smallest volume to save money.
examTraps.correction: Billing is on provisioned size and IOPS, so size/IOPS should match the requirement, not be minimized.

examTraps.trap: Assume all volumes are deleted at termination.
examTraps.correction: Only the root volume is deleted by default; other volumes persist (attribute disabled).

examTraps.trap: Say snapshotting requires the volume to be detached first.
examTraps.correction: Detaching is not necessary, only recommended.

examTraps.trap: Use Archive for a workload needing fast restore.
examTraps.correction: Archive restore takes 24 to 72 hours; use a standard snapshot (or FSR) when speed matters.

examTraps.trap: Use Fast Snapshot Restore to reduce snapshot storage cost.
examTraps.correction: FSR removes first-use latency and costs extra; use Archive for cost reduction.

examTraps.trap: Expect Recycle Bin to retain snapshots indefinitely.
examTraps.correction: Retention is set by rule and ranges from 1 day to 1 year.

examTraps.trap: Assume an unattached volume is free.
examTraps.correction: Provisioned capacity is billed whether or not the volume is attached.

beyondSource: (Tutor knowledge) The source says one instance at a time "at the CCP level"; on the SAA exam, multi-attach is a fact for specific EBS volume types (io1/io2) in the same AZ, and is still not a way to cross AZs.

(Tutor knowledge) EBS volume types (gp2/gp3, io1/io2, st1, sc1) are examinable under SAA "block storage options (HDD vs SSD)" and "selecting the appropriate storage tier"; the AZ lock and snapshot mechanics on this page apply to all of them.

sections.title: AMIs and EC2 Instance Store
sections.objective: Choose between AMI-based pre-packaged launches and EC2 Instance Store for high-IOPS, ephemeral workloads, and state why instance store data is lost on stop or hardware failure.
keyTopics: Instance store buffer and cache use cases
sections.text:
[Page 101]
AMI Overview
• 	AMI = Amazon Machine Image
• 	AMI are a 	customization 	of an EC2 instance
• 	You add your own software, configuration, operating system, monitoring…
• 	Faster boot / configuration time because all your software is pre-packaged
• 	AMI are built for a 	specific region 	(and can be copied across regions)
• 	You can launch EC2 instances from:
• 	A Public AMI: AWS provided
• 	Your own AMI: you make and maintain them yourself
• 	An AWS Marketplace AMI: an AMI someone else made (and potentially sells)

[Page 102]
AMI Process (from an EC2 instance)
• 	Start an EC2 instance and customize it
• 	Stop the instance (for data integrity)
• 	Build an AMI 	– 	this will also create EBS snapshots
• 	Launch instances from other AMIs
US-EAST-1A 	US-EAST-1B
Custom AMI

Launch

[Page 103]
EC2 Instance Store
• 	EBS volumes are 	network drives 	with good but “limited” performance
• 	If you need a high-performance hardware disk, use EC2 Instance Store
• 	Better I/O performance
• 	EC2 Instance Store lose their storage if they’re stopped (ephemeral)
• 	Good for buffer / cache / scratch data / temporary content
• 	Risk of data loss if hardware fails
• 	Backups and Replication are your responsibility

sections.title: EBS Volume Types and Multi-Attach
sections.objective: Select the EBS volume type matching IOPS, throughput, latency and cost needs, and decide when io1/io2 Multi-Attach with a cluster-aware file system is appropriate.
keyTopics: io1 and io2 Block Express PIOPS
sections.text:
[Page 105]
EBS Volume Types
• 	EBS Volumes come in 6 types
• 	gp2 / gp3 (SSD): General purpose SSD volume that balances price and performance for
a wide variety of workloads
• 	io1 / io2 Block Express (SSD): Highest-performance SSD volume for mission-critical
low-latency or high-throughput workloads
• 	st1 (HDD): Low cost HDD volume designed for frequently accessed, throughput-
intensive workloads
• 	sc1 (HDD): Lowest cost HDD volume designed for less frequently accessed workloads
• 	EBS Volumes are characterized in Size | Throughput | IOPS (I/O Ops Per Sec)
• 	When in doubt always consult the AWS documentation – it’s good!
• 	Only gp2/gp3 and io1/io2 Block Express can be used as boot volumes

[Page 106]
EBS Volume Types Use cases
General Purpose SSD
• 	Cost effective storage, low-latency
• 	System boot volumes, Virtual desktops, Development and test
environments, medium-sized databases, transactional workloads…
• 	gp3 	(1 GiB 	- 	64 TiB)
• 	Baseline of 3,000 IOPS and throughput of 125 MiB/s
• 	Can increase IOPS up to 80,000 and throughput up to 2000 MiB/s independently
• 	gp2 	(1 GiB 	- 	16 TiB)
• 	Small gp2 volumes can burst IOPS to 3,000
• 	Size of the volume and IOPS are linked, max IOPS is 16,000
• 	3 IOPS per GiB, means at 5,334 GiB we are at the max IOPS

[Page 107]
EBS Volume Types Use cases
Provisioned IOPS (PIOPS) SSD
• 	Critical business applications with sustained IOPS performance
• 	Or applications that need more than 80,000 IOPS
• 	Great for 	databases workloads 	(sensitive to storage perf and consistency)
• 	io1 	(4 GiB 	- 	16 TiB)
• 	Max PIOPS: 64,000 for Nitro EC2 instances & 32,000 for other
• 	Can increase PIOPS independently from storage size; IOPS:GiB ratio of 50:1
• 	io2 Block Express 	(4 GiB 	– 	64 TiB)
• 	Sub-millisecond latency
• 	Max PIOPS: 256,000 with an IOPS:GiB ratio of 1,000:1
• 	Supports EBS Multi-attach

[Page 108]
EBS Volume Types Use cases
Hard Disk Drives (HDD)
• 	Cannot be a boot volume
• 	125 GiB to 16 TiB
• 	Throughput Optimized HDD (st1)
• 	Big Data, Data Warehouses, Log Processing
• 	Max throughput 500 MiB/s – max IOPS 500
• 	Cold HDD (sc1):
• 	For data that is infrequently accessed
• 	Scenarios where lowest cost is important
• 	Max throughput 250 MiB/s – max IOPS 250

[Page 109]
EBS 	– Volume Types Summary
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/ebs-volume-types.html#solid-state-drives

[Page 110]
EBS Multi-Attach 	– 	io1/io2 family
• 	Attach the same EBS volume to multiple EC2
instances in the same AZ
• 	Each instance has full read & write permissions
to the high-performance volume
• 	Use case:
• 	Achieve higher application availability in clustered
Linux applications (ex: Teradata)
• 	Applications must manage concurrent write
operations
• 	Up to 16 EC2 Instances at a time
• 	Must use a file system that’s cluster-aware (not
XFS, EXT4, etc…)

sections.title: EBS Encryption and Amazon EFS
sections.objective: Explain EBS encryption at rest and its snapshot-based re-encryption path, then choose EFS versus EBS versus Instance Store based on multi-AZ sharing, OS compatibility, performance mode and cost.
keyTopics: EBS encryption at rest and in flight
Encrypting an unencrypted volume via snapshot
EBS vs EFS vs Instance Store
sections.text:
[Page 111]
EBS Encryption
• 	When you create an encrypted EBS volume, you get the following:
• 	Data at rest is encrypted inside the volume
• 	All the data in flight moving between the instance and the volume is encrypted
• 	All snapshots are encrypted
• 	All volumes created from the snapshot
• 	Encryption and decryption are handled transparently (you have nothing to
do)
• 	Encryption has a minimal impact on latency
• 	EBS Encryption leverages keys from KMS (AES-256)
• 	Copying an unencrypted snapshot allows encryption
• 	Snapshots of encrypted volumes are encrypted

[Page 112]
Encryption: encrypt an unencrypted EBS volume
• 	Create an EBS snapshot of the volume
• 	Encrypt the EBS snapshot ( using copy )
• 	Create new 	ebs 	volume from the snapshot ( the volume will also be
encrypted )
• 	Now you can attach the encrypted volume to the original instance

[Page 113]
Amazon EFS 	– 	Elastic File System
• 	Managed NFS (network file system) that can be mounted on many EC2
• 	EFS works with EC2 instances in multi-AZ
• 	Highly available, scalable, expensive (3x gp2), pay per use

[Page 114]
Amazon EFS 	– 	Elastic File System
• 	Use cases: content management, web serving, data sharing, Wordpress
• 	Uses NFSv4.1 protocol
• 	Uses security group to control access to EFS
• 	Compatible with Linux based AMI (not Windows)
• 	Encryption at rest using KMS
• 	POSIX file system (~Linux) that has a standard file API
• 	File system scales automatically, pay-per-use, no capacity planning!

[Page 115]
EFS 	– 	Performance & Storage Classes
• 	EFS Scale
• 	1000s of concurrent NFS clients, 10 GB+ /s throughput
• 	Grow to Petabyte-scale network file system, automatically
• 	Performance Mode (set at EFS creation time)
• 	General Purpose (default) – latency-sensitive use cases (web server, CMS, etc…)
• 	Max I/O – higher latency, throughput, highly parallel (big data, media processing)
• 	Throughput Mode
• 	Bursting – 1 TB = 50MiB/s + burst of up to 100MiB/s
• 	Provisioned – set your throughput regardless of storage size, ex: 1 GiB/s for 1 TB storage
• 	Elastic – automatically scales throughput up or down based on your workloads
• 	Up to 3GiB/s for reads and 1GiB/s for writes
• 	Used for unpredictable workloads

[Page 116]
EFS 	– 	Storage Classes
• 	Storage Tiers (lifecycle management feature – move
file after N days)
• 	Standard: for frequently accessed files
• 	Infrequent access (EFS-IA): cost to retrieve files, lower price
to store.
• 	Archive: rarely accessed data (few times each year), 50%
cheaper
• 	Implement lifecycle policies to move files between storage
tiers
• 	Availability and durability
• 	Standard: Multi-AZ, great for prod
• 	One Zone: One AZ, great for dev, backup enabled by
default, compatible with IA (EFS One Zone-IA)
• 	Over 90% in cost savings

EBS vs EFS 	– 	Elastic Block Storage
• 	EBS volumes…
• 	one instance (except multi-attach io1/io2)
• 	are locked at the Availability Zone (AZ) level
• 	gp2: IO increases if the disk size increases
• 	gp3 & io1: can increase IO independently
• 	To migrate an EBS volume across AZ
• 	Take a snapshot
• 	Restore the snapshot to another AZ
• 	EBS backups use IO and you shouldn’t run
them while your application is handling a lot
of traffic
• 	Root EBS Volumes of instances get
terminated by default if the EC2 instance
gets terminated. (you can disable that)
